pages.text: The assembly bell rang, and the whole school stood in neat lines. At the gate, Bismark sprinted in, tie flapping, shoes dusty, and skidded to a stop in front of Linda the prefect. “Fifth time this month!” she said, flipping open her notebook. “Name, please.” Bismark gasped for air. “You already know my name, Linda,” he said. A few students giggled.

pages.text: Linda marched Bismark to the line, and the school recited the national pledge and sang the anthem. Bismark sang it with his whole heart, still panting. When assembly ended, Mr Acquah the housemaster called him over. “Bismark, you have a reputation,” he said. “The early bird catches the worm, and you catch the bell. Before I write anything, tell me one thing. Why?”

pages.alt: A school assembly with students saluting the flag, and a housemaster calling a boy over afterwards.

pages.text: Bismark looked at his shoes. “Sir, I get up at four,” he said. “My mother sells onions at the roadside stall, and I help her set up before school. Then I walk the five kilometres here. Sometimes the trotro does not come. I try my best.” Mr Acquah listened without interrupting. Linda, standing nearby, stopped writing. She had not known any of this.

pages.alt: A boy tying up bunches of onions at a roadside stall in the grey light of dawn.

pages.text: “You should have told us,” said Mr Acquah. “Rules matter, and so do reasons. Punctuality is a habit, but a good school looks for the cause before it hands out the cane of blame.” He turned to Linda. “A prefect’s job is to guide, not to catch people out.” Linda nodded slowly. “Sorry, Bismark,” she said. “I should have asked before I assumed.”

pages.text: Together they made a plan. Bismark’s mother would let him leave the stall at five, because her neighbour’s niece offered to help. Bismark would set two alarms and pack his bag the night before. And Linda would meet him at the gate each morning for two weeks. “Think of it as turning over a new leaf,” said Mr Acquah. “Small changes, steady effort.”

pages.alt: Three people review a timetable on a notice board with a clock showing five o’clock.

pages.text: Two weeks later, Bismark arrived at 7:10, then 7:05, then 6:58. Linda cheered from the gate. By the third week he was early enough to help water the school garden. “Look at you,” said Linda. “Top of the class for punctuality!” Bismark grinned. “All thanks to you and the housemaster,” he said. “And two alarm clocks, and one very patient mother.”

pages.text: That weekend, Bismark wrote a letter to his cousin Nana in Kumasi. At the top he put his address and the date. “House 9, Market Lane, Ejisu. 6th June, 2027. Dear Nana, I hope this letter finds you and everyone at home in good health. I have good news to share. After a rough start to the term, I am now one of the first students at school each morning. My mother and my housemaster helped me find a plan that works. How is your new school? Please write soon. Your loving cousin, Bismark.”

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: in the letter, Bismark used full words, correct spelling and friendly phrases such as “I hope this letter finds you in good health” and “Please write soon.” That is the kind of informal English that fits a BECE letter to a cousin. Linda read the letter over his shoulder and smiled. “That is a lot better than a late mark,” she said. The end.
